story.title: International Criminal Court Votes to Remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan
story.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) has voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. The decision comes nearly two years after the allegations first emerged. Khan has denied the accusations, which include claims of engaging in an improper relationship with a junior staff member and attempting to prevent her from pursuing her complaint.

explore_lenses.label: Why does Khan’s removal matter for the ICC?
explore_lenses.title: A leadership crisis during major cases
explore_lenses.summary: The removal is the first of an ICC chief prosecutor and comes while the court faces intense external pressure and continues investigations and cases across several conflicts. The court says its prosecution work will continue under its deputy prosecutors.

claims.text: The Assembly of States Parties removed Khan after finding serious misconduct and a serious breach of duty; Article 46 of the Rome Statute permits removal of a prosecutor by an absolute majority of member states.
The ICC said its two deputy prosecutors will continue leading, managing and directing the Office of the Prosecutor, as they had during Khan’s leave and suspension.
Khan’s departure does not itself cancel existing arrest warrants, including those issued for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant; ICC judges, not the prosecutor, decide whether to withdraw warrants.
Human Rights Watch said the decision should reinforce that senior ICC officials are accountable for misconduct and that the court needs credible workplace protections for people reporting abuse.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a removal vote?
explore_lenses.title: A two-year disciplinary process
explore_lenses.summary: The allegations became public in 2024 and were followed by an external U.N. investigation, an internal oversight process and Khan’s June 2026 suspension before the Assembly’s July 24 vote. Khan has consistently denied wrongdoing and disputes the fairness of the procedure.

claims.text: Reporting on the disciplinary record says the allegations concerned an alleged inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior lawyer and alleged efforts to prevent her from pursuing a complaint; the Assembly’s Bureau recommended removal in June 2026.
On July 24, 2026, member states voted 82 in favor, 13 against and 15 abstentions—above the absolute-majority threshold for removal of a prosecutor.
Khan’s lawyer, Tayab Ali, said Khan had not been given a fair opportunity to be heard and that the decision defied conclusions reached by independent judges who reviewed the evidential record.

ICC law requires that an official facing a removal challenge have an opportunity to present and receive evidence and make submissions, though it does not resolve the parties’ dispute over whether that protection was adequately provided here.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next at the prosecutor’s office?
explore_lenses.title: Deputies lead while states choose a successor
explore_lenses.summary: The deputy prosecutors are running the office for now, while the Assembly of States Parties must eventually choose a new prosecutor. Khan says he will challenge the result, but the practical scope and outcome of any challenge remain unresolved.

claims.text: The Rome Statute provides that deputy prosecutors may carry out acts required of the prosecutor, and that the Office of the Prosecutor must operate independently of outside instructions.
A new prosecutor is elected by secret ballot and requires an absolute majority of Assembly of States Parties members; the statute sets the normal term at nine years.
Khan’s lawyer said he intends to challenge the lawfulness and fairness of the removal through available legal mechanisms.
AP reported that the ICC’s governing texts do not provide an appeal from a removal decision, while staff may bring employment complaints to a Geneva-based labor tribunal.

related_stories.title: Trump Issues Order for Warnings on 'Inaccurate' History at Smithsonian
related_stories.summary: President Donald Trump has issued an executive order requiring the installation of signage at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. The signs will warn visitors about what the administration deems 'inaccurate historical information' within the museum. This move follows ongoing accusations from the Trump administration of anti-American bias in the museum's exhibits.

related_stories.title: Indian Education Minister Resigns Amid Youth Protests Over Exam Scandal
related_stories.summary: Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned as India's education minister following widespread protests by youth over exam paper leaks. The protests, led by a movement referred to as 'Cockroach,' culminated in celebrations among demonstrators after Pradhan's resignation was announced. The movement's leaders indicated that the government had accepted their demands, leading to the decision to end the protests.

related_stories.title: Democrats Select South Carolina for First Presidential Primary in 2028
related_stories.summary: The Democratic National Committee has recommended that South Carolina hold the first presidential primary for the 2028 election cycle. This decision marks a significant shift in the primary calendar, as South Carolina will replace Iowa as the opening contest. The move aims to prioritize representation among Black and Latino voters, with Nevada also scheduled for an early primary.

related_stories.title: Maine Democrats Set to Nominate Troy Jackson for Senate Race
related_stories.summary: Maine Democrats are convening to select a Senate nominee to replace Graham Platner, with former state Senate President Troy Jackson expected to secure the nomination. Jackson, who comes from a logging family, is preparing to challenge Republican Senator Susan Collins in the upcoming election, which is being closely watched nationally. Collins has significantly outpaced Jackson in fundraising, raising over $16 million compared to Jackson's $1 million since entering the race.
